project_name: Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems
initial_requirements: The Ministry of Home Affairs needs a Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems application to improve day-to-day police work and support better crime investigation and criminal detection. The system will be used by investigating officers, records staff, and citizens. It should provide an initial foundation for registering complaints, supporting investigations, and exchanging relevant information between police units and the public.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. My goal is to understand your needs clearly so we can define the right system for Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems.

Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do you expect something different from it?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, I’m in line with that scope. We want to understand what the system should do for complaint registration, investigation support, and information sharing between police staff and citizens. That should be enough to start, and then we can go into the details step by step.

turns.interviewer_utterance: To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I’m here as a stakeholder representing the policing and records side of the project. My concern is making sure the system supports day-to-day police work, helps investigating officers, and gives citizens a practical way to register and track complaints.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Thank you. To begin with the current situation, can you describe the existing process or system you use today for registering complaints, handling investigations, and sharing information between police staff and citizens?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Right now it’s mostly a mix of manual paperwork, local registers, and some disconnected computer files in different units. A citizen usually has to visit the station, the complaint gets written down, and then the records staff or officer follows up through phone calls, paper files, or local contacts. Because the information isn’t centralized, tracking a case across units or sharing updates with the citizen can be slow and sometimes inconsistent.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current processes do you want to change or improve first in this project?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The first thing we want to improve is complaint registration and tracking, because that is the entry point for most cases. After that, we want better visibility for investigating officers so they can follow a case without chasing paper files, and we also want citizens to get clearer status updates. The information sharing between police units is important too, but I would say the complaint flow is the biggest pain point right now.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Based on your description, do you think citizen self-service complaint submission should also be included, or should complaints still always be entered by police or records staff?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, citizen self-service should be included if possible, because it would reduce queues at the station and make it easier for people to report issues. But I don’t think it should replace police entry completely, since some complainants may not be comfortable online or may need help from staff. So we would need both options: citizens can submit themselves, and staff can still enter complaints on their behalf.

turns.interviewer_utterance: So these are the main features/functions I understand so far: complaint registration and tracking, investigation visibility for officers, citizen status updates, information sharing between police units, citizen self-service complaint submission, and staff-assisted complaint entry. Is that correct?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, that’s correct. Those are the main functions we need at this stage. If we can cover those well, it would already make a big difference to how the system works day to day.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Are there any other main features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something that has not been the primary focus so far?
turns.interviewee_utterance: One additional feature we would likely need is search and retrieval of past cases, because officers and records staff often need to check whether something was reported before. It would also be useful to have basic reporting or dashboards for management, so they can see case volumes and progress. Beyond that, I think those would be secondary to the core complaint and investigation functions.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Based on your description, do you think notification alerts for complaint status changes or officer actions should also be included?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, I think notifications should be included. They would be very useful for both citizens and officers, especially when a complaint is assigned, updated, or closed. We would just need to keep them simple and reliable, so people actually get the updates without creating extra noise.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the confirmed main features in order of importance?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The highest priority is complaint registration and tracking, including staff-assisted entry and citizen self-service. Next would be investigation visibility for officers and notification alerts, because those help move cases forward and keep everyone informed. After that, I would place citizen status updates, information sharing between police units, and then search and retrieval of past cases, with basic reporting or dashboards following that.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the highest-priority feature, complaint registration and tracking, can you describe what information must be captured when a complaint is created?
turns.interviewee_utterance: At a minimum, we need the complainant’s name, contact details, the date and time of the incident, the place where it happened, and a short description of what occurred. If the person is reporting on behalf of someone else, that relationship should also be captured. It would also be helpful to assign a complaint number immediately so the case can be tracked from the start.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want complaint registration and tracking to accomplish beyond just storing the details.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should do more than store details; it should create a clear workflow for the case from receipt to closure. That means the complaint can be assigned to the right officer or unit, its status can be updated as action is taken, and staff can see whether it is pending, under investigation, or resolved. We would also want an audit trail so we know who handled it and when changes were made.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need complaint assignment, status tracking, and an audit trail. Can you describe more about how a complaint should be assigned and who is allowed to change its status?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Assignment should usually be done by records staff or a supervising officer, based on the type of complaint, location, and urgency. In some urgent cases, an investigating officer may be assigned immediately, but the system should still keep that controlled. Status changes should be limited to authorized police staff, especially the assigned officer and their supervisor, while citizens should only be able to view updates, not change them.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current system or process, if any, do you use today for complaint numbering, assignment, and status updates?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Right now, in many places it is still handled manually or with a very basic register, sometimes even in spreadsheets. Complaint numbers may be written in sequence from a station logbook, and assignment is often done by a supervisor based on availability and judgment. Status updates are usually shared informally or entered later, so there is not always a single reliable system of record.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within complaint registration and tracking, such as complaint numbering, assignment, status updates, and audit trail?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Complaint numbering comes first because every case needs a unique reference immediately. After that, assignment and status updates are the most important since they drive the actual handling of the complaint and keep the case moving. The audit trail is also essential, but I would place it just after those because it supports accountability and review rather than the core day-to-day flow.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the citizen self-service complaint submission feature, what should a citizen be able to do from their side?
turns.interviewee_utterance: A citizen should be able to submit a complaint online, attach basic supporting documents or photos if they have them, and receive a reference number after submission. They should also be able to check the current status of their complaint using that reference number. If needed, they should be able to view basic guidance on what information to provide, but not edit an already submitted complaint unless staff approve it.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what citizen self-service should accomplish beyond submitting and viewing a complaint.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should reduce the need for a person to come physically to the station for every minor update, and it should make the process feel transparent. Ideally, the citizen can see that the complaint was received, assigned, and is being looked into, without having to call repeatedly. It should also help them feel confident that their report is officially recorded and not lost.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need online submission, attachment upload, reference number generation, and citizen status tracking. Can you describe more about what kind of attachments should be allowed and whether there should be any limits?
turns.interviewee_utterance: We would allow common supporting files like photos, scanned documents, and possibly short audio or video evidence if the file is relevant to the complaint. There should definitely be limits on file size and the number of attachments so the system does not get overloaded, but I do not know the exact thresholds yet. We would also want to restrict unsafe file types and keep the uploads tied securely to the complaint record.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current process, if any, do you use today for citizens submitting complaints or evidence, and how is that handled now?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Today, it is mostly done in person at the police station, or sometimes by phone and then written up by staff later. Evidence is usually brought physically on a USB, paper copy, or as printed photos, and then filed with the complaint record manually. In some cases people may send things by email or messaging apps, but that is not consistent and it is not part of one formal system.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within citizen self-service, such as online submission, attachment upload, reference number generation, status tracking, and guidance?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Online submission is the highest priority because that is the main entry point for the citizen. Reference number generation and status tracking come next, since they let the citizen follow up without repeated visits or calls. Attachment upload and guidance are also important, but I would place guidance slightly lower because it supports the process rather than being essential to the basic submission flow.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the investigation support feature, what should investigating officers be able to see or do in the system?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Investigating officers should be able to view the complaint details, see the assigned status, add investigation notes, and update the case as it progresses. They should also be able to link related people, places, vehicles, or prior incidents if that information is available. In practice, they need enough information to follow the case properly and record what they have done without relying only on paper files.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want investigation support to accomplish beyond just viewing and updating the complaint.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should help officers work the case faster and keep all the important information in one place. Ideally, they can see the complaint history, evidence, and any linked records so they do not have to search across different registers or offices. It should also make it easier for supervisors or other units to understand what has been done so far and continue the investigation if needed.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need complaint history, evidence viewing, linked records, and investigation notes. Can you describe more about who should be allowed to add or edit investigation notes and linked records?
turns.interviewee_utterance: That should be limited to investigating officers and possibly their supervisors, not general staff or citizens. Records staff might view the information, but I would not expect them to edit investigation notes unless they have been specifically assigned that role. We would need role-based access so only authorized users can change those details, and I am not sure yet whether edits should be fully open or require an audit trail.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current system or process, if any, do you use today for investigation notes, linked records, and case history?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Mostly it is handled through paper case files, station registers, and sometimes separate spreadsheets or local databases if a unit has them. Notes are written by hand or typed in reports, and linked information is often kept as references in the file rather than in a searchable way. Case history is reconstructed by checking the file movement and past entries, so it is slower and depends a lot on manual effort.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within investigation support, such as case history, evidence viewing, linked records, and investigation notes?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Case history is the most important because officers need to understand what has already happened before they act. Investigation notes come next, since that is how the team records progress and decisions. Evidence viewing and linked records are also important, but I would place them after those two because they support the investigation rather than define it.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the notification alerts feature, what events should trigger a notification and who should receive them?
turns.interviewee_utterance: A notification should go out when a complaint is submitted, when its status changes, and when an officer adds an update or requests more information. Citizens should receive alerts for their own case, and investigating officers and supervisors should receive alerts for cases assigned to them or escalated to them. If there is a missing attachment or incomplete information, that should also trigger a message to the citizen so they can respond sooner.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want notification alerts to accomplish beyond simply informing users of changes.
turns.interviewee_utterance: They should reduce delays and keep the complaint moving without people having to keep checking the system. For citizens, the alerts should tell them what action is needed, like providing more details or knowing that the complaint has been accepted. For officers, the notifications should help them react quickly to new assignments, updates, or pending follow-up so cases do not sit unattended.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need submission alerts, status change alerts, officer update alerts, and incomplete-information alerts. Can you describe more about how users should receive these notifications, for example by email, SMS, or in-app messages?
turns.interviewee_utterance: In-app messages should definitely be there for users who are already logged into the system. For citizens, SMS would be the most useful because many may not check the portal often, and email could be added where available. For officers, I would expect in-app alerts first, with email maybe as a backup, but the exact mix would depend on what communication details we have on file.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current process, if any, do you use today for notifying citizens or officers about complaint status changes and updates?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Today it is mostly done manually by phone calls, SMS from individual officers, or sometimes through follow-up visits at the station. In some places, the complainant has to come back and ask for the status themselves, which is obviously not ideal. There is no single standardized process across all units right now.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within notifications, such as event triggers, recipient groups, and delivery channels?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Event triggers are the most important because without them the alerts will not be useful. Recipient groups come next, since the system needs to know who should get each alert. Delivery channels are important too, but I would put them after those two because they are more about how the message is sent than whether the right people are informed.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For information sharing between police units, what kind of information should be shared, and between which units or roles?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Mostly case-related information should be shared, such as complaint details, suspect information, status updates, and relevant evidence references. It should go between investigating officers, records staff, and supervisors, and in some cases across nearby police units if a case moves from one jurisdiction to another. Citizens should not see internal police-to-police sharing, only the parts meant for them.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want police-unit information sharing to accomplish beyond simply letting units see the same case record.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should make sure the right unit can act quickly without waiting for papers or repeated phone calls. If a case is transferred, escalated, or needs verification from another station, the receiving unit should have enough context to continue work immediately. It also helps avoid duplication and gaps, so the investigation stays consistent as it moves between teams.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need case transfer, escalation, cross-unit context sharing, and duplicate prevention. Can you describe more about who should be allowed to initiate or approve a case transfer?
turns.interviewee_utterance: A transfer should usually be initiated by the investigating officer or the station handling the complaint, but it should not happen without some approval. I would expect a supervisor or authorized officer to approve it, especially when the case is moving to another jurisdiction. The exact approval level may depend on how serious the case is, but it should not be open to everyone.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current system or process, if any, do you use today for sharing cases between police units or transferring them across jurisdictions?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Right now it is mostly manual. Officers share details by phone, physical case files, email, or official letters when something has to move to another station or unit. There is no unified digital transfer process in place, so it can take time and sometimes important context gets lost.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within information sharing, such as cross-unit context, transfer/approval, and duplicate prevention?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Cross-unit context is the highest priority because the receiving unit needs the full picture to continue work properly. Transfer and approval come next since we need control over who can move a case and when. Duplicate prevention is also important, but I would rank it after those two because it supports accuracy rather than the actual handoff process.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the search and retrieval of past cases feature, what should users be able to search by, and what should they see in the results?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Users should be able to search by things like case number, complainant name, suspect name, date range, location, and type of offense. In the results, they should see a short summary with the case status, assigned unit, key dates, and whether any linked evidence or related complaints exist. For authorized staff, it should also open the full case record.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want past-case search and retrieval to accomplish beyond finding an old case.
turns.interviewee_utterance: It should help officers quickly understand whether a new complaint is connected to something already reported before. That way they can avoid redoing work, spot repeat offenders or patterns, and use the earlier record as supporting context during an investigation. It should also help records staff and supervisors verify history without manually digging through files.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need searchable case history, connected-case detection, and full-record access for authorized staff. Can you describe more about who should be allowed to search and who should be allowed to view the full case details?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Basic searching should be available to investigating officers and records staff, since they need to locate past cases as part of their work. Viewing the full case details should be more restricted, limited to authorized police personnel who are assigned to the case or have supervisory access. Citizens should not see full internal case details, only whatever status or complaint information we decide is safe to expose to them.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current process, if any, do you use today for searching and retrieving past cases?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Today it is still mostly manual. Staff look through register books, old files, or local station records, and sometimes they have to call another unit to confirm whether a case already exists. It works, but it is slow and depends a lot on who knows where the record is kept.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within search and retrieval, such as searchable fields, summary results, and full-record access?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Searchable fields are the most important because if staff cannot find the case quickly, nothing else matters. Summary results come next since they let the user confirm they have the right record without opening everything. Full-record access is also important, but only for authorized users, so I would place that after the basic search and summary needs.

turns.interviewer_utterance: For the basic reporting or dashboards feature, what kinds of reports or metrics should management be able to see?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Management should be able to see basic counts of complaints received, cases opened, cases closed, and cases still pending. It would also be useful to show trends by time, location, and type of crime, so they can see where pressure is building. For supervisors, a simple view of workload by unit or officer would also help.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Please elaborate on what you want reporting and dashboards to accomplish beyond just displaying numbers.
turns.interviewee_utterance: The main point is to help management make decisions faster, not just read statistics. They should be able to spot backlogs, recurring crime patterns, and areas that need more attention so they can allocate staff and resources better. It should also give them a quick operational picture without having to ask for separate manual reports every time.

turns.interviewer_utterance: It seems like you need complaint counts, trend analysis, workload views, and backlog detection. Can you describe more about who should be allowed to view these reports and dashboards?
turns.interviewee_utterance: These reports should mainly be visible to management, supervisors, and authorized senior police staff. Investigating officers may need limited views for their own unit or assigned cases, but not the full organization-wide picture unless they have permission. Citizens should not have access to internal dashboards like this.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What current process, if any, do you use today for reporting, dashboards, or management summaries?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Right now most summaries are prepared manually from station records and then compiled into spreadsheets or written reports. If a higher-level review is needed, staff usually collect information from several units and put it together by hand. It takes time and the numbers are not always available in real time.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Could you please prioritize the detailed needs within reporting and dashboards, such as counts, trends, and workload views?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Counts are the first priority because management needs the basic numbers immediately. Trends come next since they help show whether the situation is improving or getting worse over time. Workload views are also important, but I would place them after those two because they are more useful for supervision and resource planning.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?
turns.interviewee_utterance: The most important additional voices would be investigating officers, station-level supervisors, records staff, and citizens. Officers and records staff know the day-to-day process and where delays or duplicate work happen, while supervisors can speak to reporting and oversight needs. Citizens matter too because they are the ones filing complaints and checking whether the system is simple, accessible, and trustworthy.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What would make you consider this system deployment successful?
turns.interviewee_utterance: I would consider it successful if complaints can be registered faster and with fewer errors, and if officers can track cases more easily from start to finish. It should also reduce manual paperwork and make management reporting quicker and more reliable. If citizens can submit complaints and get a clear response or status update, that would also be a strong sign it is working well.

turns.interviewer_utterance: To summarize, we discussed complaint registration and tracking, citizen self-service submissions, investigation support, notification alerts, information sharing between police units, search and retrieval of past cases, and reporting dashboards. Is there anything else you would like to add?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Yes, one important addition is access control and audit trails, so we can know who viewed or changed a record and protect sensitive information properly. We would also need duplicate checking and strong search so staff can quickly find related complaints or repeat offenders. If possible, the system should also be designed to work reliably in police stations even when connectivity is not ideal.

turns.interviewer_utterance:
Thanks for those additions. Based on our discussion, I will prepare a detailed summary for review and note the follow-up items: access control and audit trails, duplicate checking, and offline/reliable operation in low-connectivity stations.

Who else do you think should review or validate these requirements before we finalize them?
turns.interviewee_utterance: Station supervisors and senior investigating officers should definitely review them because they understand operational control and approval needs. Records staff should also validate the complaint handling and search flows since they will use it every day. I think the IT or security team should check the access control, audit trail, and connectivity requirements before we finalize anything.
